literal_edits.before: [F5] [[lem-convergent-power-series-termwise-differentiation]]: if a power series and its formal derivative series converge absolutely at every smaller radius, the sum differentiates termwise inside the radius.
literal_edits.after: [F5] [[thm-termwise-differentiation-of-complex-power-series]]: a complex power series is holomorphic inside its disk of convergence and its complex derivative is the sum of its formal derivative series.

literal_edits.before: Thus the original and derivative series satisfy the absolute-convergence hypotheses of [F5] at every smaller radius, so $T,U$ differentiate termwise there and the formal identities hold for their analytic sums.
literal_edits.after: The radii of convergence of $T,U$ are therefore at least $e^{-1}$, and [F5] makes both sums holomorphic and termwise complex differentiable throughout $|z|<e^{-1}$.

3.2 Fix $|z|<e^{-1}$ and put $S=\sum_{k\ge1}a_k|z|^k<\infty$. The Cauchy products in step 2.1 are absolutely summable, dominated by products of the corresponding absolute series from step 3.1. Expanding $T(z)^m$ gives absolute sum at most $S^m$, so the full exponential composition is dominated by $\sum_{m\ge0}S^m/m!<\infty$; this last series is $1$ when $S=0$, and for $S>0$ its successive-term ratio $S/(m+1)$ tends to zero. These summable majorants control all omitted terms, so finite polynomial expansions may be passed to the limit and regrouped by powers of $z$. The formal identities in steps 1.1 and 2.1 therefore give $T=ze^T$, $zT'(1-T)=T$, and $zU'=T$ for the analytic sums. If $T(z)=1$, the first identity forces $z=e^{-1}$, outside the disk; hence $1-T(z)\ne0$, and division gives $zT'=T/(1-T)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]
